name: Dihydroxyacetone
lead: Dihydroxyacetone (DHA, also called glycerone) is a three-carbon sugar and the active ingredient in most sunless tanning lotions, sprays, mousses, wipes and salon spray tans [1][3]. It gives skin a golden-to-deep brown colour within hours, without ultraviolet exposure, by reacting with amino acids in the outermost layer of the skin to form brown pigments called melanoidins; the colour is a surface stain rather than new melanin [1][21].

People use it to add a tan to the face and body for events, photos and everyday looks, to even out pale or uneven skin tone, and to add shadow and definition to a physique. Colour appears after two to four hours, deepens over one to three days and fades over roughly three to ten days as the stained skin cells shed [1][23]. Drugstore products typically contain about 3 to 5 percent DHA and professional products 5 to 20 percent, with stronger concentrations giving darker results [1].

The US FDA permits DHA as a colour additive for external application but not for the eyes, lips, mucous membranes, inhalation or ingestion, and has not approved it as an all-over spray or mist in booths; sunless tanners without sunscreen cannot claim protection from ultraviolet radiation [22][3]. Reviews note that more safety studies are warranted given how widespread its use is [3][4].

In looksmaxxing communities DHA self-tanner is discussed as a way to add colour without UV exposure, with threads on application mistakes, facial products, mole concerns and comparisons with peptide tanning [16][17][19][20].

paras: DHA is used to give a temporary tan on the face and body. Formulations include sprays, lotions, gels, mousses, drops that are mixed into moisturiser, and cosmetic wipes, and salon applications include spray booths, airbrushing and hand-applied products. Lotions often last longer than sprays but may cause blotching and streaking, while mousses and gels tend to dry faster [1].

Preparation described in reference sources includes shaving, washing or exfoliating beforehand, limiting moisturiser to very dry areas, and applying in circular motions to reduce streaks [1]. Colour builds over 24 to 72 hours and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, a spray tan lasts about five to ten days; dermatologist Jennifer Lucas told the clinic that it is 'not a base tan' and does not protect against sunburn [23]. Wikipedia notes that tanners often contain other colour ingredients such as erythrulose (a slower-acting reddish tan agent), walnut shell extract and so-called tyrosine 'optimizers', whose effectiveness is disputed [1].

Face application is a frequent topic because colour on the face is the most visible and the most unforgiving of streaks at the hairline, eyes and mouth [16]. Many users choose a dedicated facial formula or drops blended with their usual moisturiser to control depth [19].

A review of vitiligo camouflage lists DHA among temporary concealment options [6]. Early research on DHA's skin colouring in the 1950s arose from observations in children given oral DHA for a glycogen storage disease [1]. A 1976 trial treated 30 photosensitive patients with a DHA and lawsone sunscreen [7], and a randomized study and registered trial have examined DHA for visible-light protection in erythropoietic protoporphyria [8][13].

German scientists recognised DHA as a skin-colouring agent in the 1920s after noticing browning when it was spilled during X-ray processing [1]. In the 1950s Eva Wittgenstein at the University of Cincinnati researched DHA, noting that children given large oral doses for glycogen storage disease developed brown skin where it was spilled, and she then painted solutions on her own skin [1][21]. Research later explored DHA for vitiligo camouflage [1][6].

Man-Tan (1959) was the first commercial DHA self-tanner, followed by Coppertone's Quick Tan (1960) [21][1]. Many consumers disliked results such as orange palms and streaking, which shaped lingering associations with fake-looking tans [1][21]. The FDA added DHA to its list of approved cosmetic colour additives in the 1970s, and improved formulations appeared in the 1980s as concern over UV tanning grew [1]. From the late 1990s, automated spray-tan booths broadened the market [21].

Studies in humans have examined DHA's colouring and any photoprotective effect. A 2004 trial letter and a 2005 controlled study examined sunlight protection from DHA-induced Maillard-reaction pigments [10][9]. A 1976 clinical trial reported that a DHA-lawsone sunscreen protected 30 patients with various light sensitivities, with about 80 percent experiencing enough protection for a near-normal summer lifestyle [7]. A 2023 randomized trial examined protection against visible light by DHA in erythropoietic protoporphyria [8], with a small registered follow-up [13].

Reviews state that sunless tanning products are regulated as cosmetics that cannot claim protection from UV, whereas earlier reviews describe DHA and melanins as providing some photoprotection [3][5]. Wikipedia reports a 2007 study (Jung and colleagues) finding that DHA-treated skin produced more free radicals under sun exposure, and the article advises sun protection for roughly a day after application [21]. It also reports a Mutation Research study finding DNA damage from DHA in cultured cells [21]. No large randomized trials of DHA self-tanner compare appearance outcomes against other tanning routes.

DHA condenses with amino-acid residues of keratin in the stratum corneum; the resulting melanoidins resemble melanin in colour and can be removed by abrasion. When injected, no pigmentation occurs, consistent with a role for oxygen in colour development [1]. It was initially thought not to penetrate past the stratum corneum, though the FDA later concluded this is not entirely true [1].

DHA is a hygroscopic white crystalline powder and the simplest ketose, with no chiral centre. It normally exists as a dimer that converts to the monomer in water, and solutions are stable at pH 4 to 6 but degrade to brown products in basic solution [1]. It is prepared by mild oxidation of glycerol or by fermentation, and can be derived from sugar beets and sugar cane [1][2]. Its phosphorylated form takes part in glycolysis [1].

Reported effects of spray tans include rashes, and mainly with spray booths, coughing, dizziness and fainting; the FDA notes the cause of these reports is uncertain [22][1]. Frequent exposure has been associated in the reference literature with possible respiratory risks, and fragrances and preservatives in formulations may cause allergic reactions or contact dermatitis [1][21].

A systematic review of self-tanning agents notes concerns about DHA cytotoxicity, genotoxicity and systemic absorption [15]. Reviews describe safety data on inhalation and long-term use as limited [3][4]. An FDA report is cited as estimating that a small share of applied DHA may penetrate living skin layers, and the Cleveland Clinic says an FDA report suggests a small amount can enter the bloodstream [1][23]. In pregnancy, MotherToBaby reports laboratory models suggesting less than 1 percent of DHA is absorbed and says no studies have examined sunless tanners and pregnancy outcomes [24].

The FDA lists DHA as a colour additive permitted for external application and not for the eye area, lips or other mucous membranes, or for inhalation or ingestion. It has not approved DHA as an all-over spray in booths and advises customers to ask salons how eyes, mucous membranes and inhalation are protected [22]. Products without sunscreen must carry a warning that they do not protect against sunburn [22]. The agency does not approve cosmetics before sale, and salons are generally overseen by state and local authorities [22].

Wikipedia reports that a 2010 EU Scientific Committee opinion found no risk from DHA spray tanning and has been criticised for relying heavily on unpublished studies with industry links [21]. Unlicensed melanotan products, sometimes discussed as alternatives, are described there as not legal in any jurisdiction, with health agencies warning against them since 2007 [21].

Temporary bronzers wash off with soap and water and typically use colorants such as caramel or walnut extracts; many are makeup-like tinted moisturisers or powders [22][21]. Erythrulose works like DHA but more slowly [21]. Oral carotenoids can alter skin colour with chronic high intake, though beta-carotene and canthaxanthin pills are not approved for tanning and canthaxanthin has been linked to liver and eye problems [21]. Melanotan-type peptides, which stimulate melanin production, are discussed in forums as a different route to a tan [17][21].

On looksmax.org, threads include requests for help fixing streaky facial applications, product recommendations, questions about dose for self-tanning drops, and discussion of whether self-tanners suit people with many moles [16][18][19][20][17]. Some users recommend exfoliating with a scrub to remove uneven colour [16]. In one thread a poster asking about tanning with many moles was told to use melanotan 2, and another user replied that melanotan also raises melanocyte activity and may darken moles [17].

lore.intro: DHA is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a practical, low-commitment tanning option, often compared with sun exposure and melanotan [17][20].

claims.claim: Self-tanner is a safe alternative to UV tanning
claims.believers: Users who worry about moles ask about self-tanning as a way to colour skin without sun [17].
claims.experts: The FDA permits topical use but not near eyes or mucous membranes; reviews say long-term and inhalation safety data are limited, and a dermatologist told the Cleveland Clinic that self-tanning is not risk-free but involves no UV [22][3][4][23].

claims.believers: Not widely claimed in the sampled forum threads, though earlier reviews credit DHA with some photoprotection [5].
claims.experts: The FDA states sunless tanners are cosmetics and cannot protect against UV [3].

claims.claim: Streaks and blotches can be removed by scrubbing
claims.believers: A reply recommends an abrasive scrub of salt or sugar with oil for uneven colour on the face [16].
claims.experts: DHA pigments sit in the stratum corneum and can be removed by abrasion [1].

claims.claim: Face application needs care around eyes, mouth and hairline
claims.believers: A user describes white patches left at the eye area, mouth and hairline after uneven application [16].
claims.experts: FDA guidance excludes eyes, lips and mucous membranes [3].

claims.claim: Self-tanners are 'cope' compared to real tanning
claims.believers: The thread title asks whether self-tanners are 'cope'; replies focus on mole risk from sun and peptides [17].
claims.experts: DHA gives a surface colour that fades as skin exfoliates; no study compares it with other tanning routes for perceived attractiveness [1].

claims.claim: A higher DHA percentage gives a darker, longer-lasting tan
claims.believers: Users discuss stronger formulas and repeated layering to deepen colour, and warn about streaks from heavy application [16][19].
claims.experts: Reference sources say higher concentrations give darker results with greater risk of streaking, and colour deepens over 24 to 72 hours before fading over days [1][23].

claims.claim: Melanotan or peptides are a better route to a tan than self-tanner
claims.believers: A reply in a mole-concern thread recommends melanotan 2 to tan with many moles [17].
claims.experts: Another user in that thread notes melanotan raises melanocyte activity and may darken moles; Wikipedia says unlicensed melanotan products are not legal in any jurisdiction and have drawn health-agency warnings since 2007 [17][21].

chain: Apply DHA product to clean, exfoliated skin
DHA reacts with keratin in the outer skin layer within hours
Brown melanoidin colour develops and deepens over one to three days
Temporary tan that fades as the outer skin sheds over about a week
angle.text: DHA gives a visible tan on the day it is applied and builds in depth over the following days. People use it on the face and body for colour, even tone and a more defined look, choosing sprays, mousses, lotions, drops or salon applications depending on how dark and how natural they want the result.
